newsitem.title: FRANCE: OPINION - CSA analysis of its French opinion poll.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - CSA analysis of its French opinion poll.

text.p: The following article was contributed by Stephane Rozes, head of political studies and opinion polling at the CSA Institute. CSA late on Monday published the first poll of voters' intentions since President Jacques Chirac called a snap election for May 25 and June 1.
The opinions expressed in this column represent those of the author alone. The article was translated from French by Reuters.

PARIS, April 23 - A majority of the French people remain sceptical about President Jacques Chirac's Monday announcement that he was dissolving the National Assembly and calling an early parliamentary election. Fifty-seven percent of those polled (1) on April 22 thought he had not been "convincing", while 40 percent had the opposite view.

Eighty-one percent of those polled perceived the announcement as a political move. While 72 percent think it is a good way to "let the French express themselves", they don't see it as a way to actually improve the country's situation or reduce unemployment. Moreover, some fear a new government would impose further austerity on the country.
NO SHIFT IN THE BALANCE OF FORCES
President Chirac's decision however has not triggered a deep change in the balance of political forces for the time being.

If the election were to take place today, the UDF/RPR (centre-right) majority would remain in power with 43 percent of the votes and 332 seats. The Socialists and other parties on the Left would get 28 percent of the votes and have 201 seats while the Communist party would get 20 seats with nine percent of the votes.
The Ecologists and the National Front would win a seat each, with 6 percent and 13 percent of the vote, respectively.

In comparison with our previous opinion polls, we see that the Socialists are still sliding, and although they had 27 percent of voting intentions in May 1996, they had just 22 percent on April 22, 1997, while the ruling coalition had risen to 37 percent from 29 percent.
The most notable change since the previous poll, conducted on April 7 and 8 is the decline of the National Front's score to 13 percent from 16 percent.

It appears as if Jacques Chirac's decision to shake up the political landscape, asserting his desire to reinforce his majority by urging a new forward momentum, has pleased some National Front voters.
SOCIALISTS WILL HAVE TO ASSERT THEMSELVES QUICKLY

The main conclusion of this first poll is that it is not enough for the Socialists simply to point out that the French are dissatisfied with their situation and critical of their government to be seen as a natural alternative.
The French expect the left-wing opposition to define its position with respect to the current government, but above all to embody a credible alternative able to bring about change.

This shows that they will be hard-pressed, in the few weeks remaining before the first round of the election, to transform their opposition status into a programme which responds to the French peoples' concerns and demonstrate their ability to be a political force, both domestically and in Europe.
(1) The poll was conducted for Le Parisien, France Inter and France Info on April 22 1997, from a representative sample of 1,002 people aged 18 and over.
